tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

12	- **No new record kind and no `model.rs` change is needed.** A browser is
13	  one more `PairedDevice` (`src/ports/remote.rs:96-107`: `id`, `name`,
14	  `scope`, `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen`) in
15	  `<data dir>/devices.json`. That file is a bare `Vec<PairedDevice>`
16	  with no schema version (`RemoteFiles::load_devices`/`save_devices`,
17	  `src/adapters/remote.rs:80-86`), written atomically by
18	  `Effect::SaveDevices` (`src/core/remote.rs:121-125`). The name comes
19	  from `/pair`'s `device_name` (`src/app.rs:3650-3655`), cut to 64 chars
20	  in `AppCore::new_device` (`src/core/remote.rs:166-175`). So "Safari on
21	  iPhone" can be the page's own `device_name` with no host change. If
22	  the plan wants a `kind` (browser or native) on the device, it is an
23	  additive `#[serde(default)]` field in a file that has no version.
24	- **Rehydration** is unchanged: `IdentityLoaded { identity, devices,
25	  rotated }` (`src/core/remote.rs:22-30`) puts the devices back at
26	  launch. A token is checked by hash against them on every request
27	  (`authenticate`, `src/app.rs:3125-3153`; `device_by_token`,
28	  `src/core/remote.rs:145-147`). Revoke (`RevokeDevice`,
29	  `src/core/remote.rs:86-92`) and scope change (`:93-100`) apply on the
30	  next request, and revoke closes the device's socket (test
31	  `revoke_closes_the_devices_socket`, `tests/remote.rs:2892`).
32	- **The pairing window is not durable** (`PairingWindow` in core state:
33	  code, scope, `until`, failures; `OpenPairing`/`ClosePairing`/
34	  `PairingFailed`/`Paired`, `src/core/remote.rs:46-73`). The QR is built
35	  in the UI from it (`src/ui/remote.rs:155-173`). Changing JSON to a URL
36	  is a change to that `json!` call and to the "Copy invite" text (`:199-206`),
37	  not to any record.
38	- **The page itself is not a record.** It is static bytes compiled in
39	  (`include_str!`). On the device, what persists is the token, plus
40	  whatever the page keeps to say "identity changed". Decision 2 picks
41	  where that is. The browser also keeps its certificate exception per
42	  host. The host keeps nothing new per browser beyond the device record.
43	- **Identity** (`identity.json`, `Identity` at `src/ports/remote.rs:26-42`,
44	  `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1` at `:17`). It holds the certificate
45	  (base64 DER) and `spki_sha256`. The certificate is made by
46	  `make_identity` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`) with
47	  `CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())`: **no subjectAltName at
48	  all**, a CN of `Switchboard <server_id>`, rcgen's default validity
49	  (the comment says `not_after` is the year 4096), and no EKU set
50	  explicitly. The native clients pin the SPKI and ignore names, so this
51	  never mattered. A browser checks names and validity. Changing the
52	  certificate (adding SANs for the LAN address or a `.local` name, or a
53	  bounded validity) changes nothing the pin sees if the key is reused
54	  (the SPKI is the same, §5). But the certificate is stored in
55	  `identity.json`, so reissuing it means writing that file, and an
56	  address that moves would need another reissue.

58	## What the code does today, piece by piece
59	
60	### The listener (`src/adapters/remote.rs`)
61	
62	- `read_request` (`:444-513`) keeps the method, the path, the query
63	  (undecoded), the body, `bearer` (`Authorization: Bearer`, `:487-491`)
64	  and `upgrade` (`Sec-WebSocket-Key` when `Upgrade: websocket`,
65	  `:492-495`). It throws away every other header. **It does not read
66	  `Cookie`, `Origin`, `User-Agent`, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, `Host`,
67	  `If-None-Match` or `Accept`.** Either token transport in decision 2
68	  needs a new `RemoteRequest` field. That struct is in
69	  `src/adapters/remote.rs:359-372`, which is not under `ports/`, but
70	  `tests/remote.rs` builds requests and should be checked.
71	- `respond` (`:530-552`) always writes `Content-Type: application/json`
72	  and `Connection: keep-alive`, nothing else. It has no CSP, no
73	  Cache-Control, no Set-Cookie and no other content type. `RemoteReply`
74	  (`:388-393`) is `{status, body, authenticated}`. Static files and a
75	  cookie on `/pair` therefore need `RemoteReply` (or a separate
76	  connection-thread path) to carry headers. `respond_upgrade`
77	  (`:519-527`) writes no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. A browser that offered
78	  a subprotocol fails the handshake if the server does not echo one
79	  (that is a question below, not checked).
80	- Pools and windows: `MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED = 4`, `MAX_PAIRED = 12`
81	  (`:567-568`). A stream past the 4 is dropped at accept (`:699-706`). A
82	  connection moves pools only when a reply says `authenticated: true`
83	  (`:834-849`). `HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT` is 5 s (`:570`), and the first
84	  request line has the same deadline. `IDLE_TIMEOUT` is 30 s (`:573`).
85	  The rate windows exist only for `/api/v1/pair` (6/min) and
86	  `/api/v1/info` (60/min) (`:583-587`, `Limits::limited` `:629-640`).
87	  Any other path, a static one included, is unlimited and goes to the
88	  frame. What this means for a page load: a browser opens several
89	  parallel connections and keeps them alive. Static GETs leave a
90	  connection in the unauthenticated pool for up to 30 s idle. A
91	  failed TLS handshake (the certificate warning) also holds a slot until
92	  it ends. **The pool of 4 is what an unpaired page load competes for.**
93	  Once paired, each fetch with the cookie or token moves its connection
94	  to the paired pool. The test `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool_and_never_a_paired_clients`
95	  (`tests/remote.rs:3226`) is the existing model for that behaviour.
96	- The frame drain: `port.poll(DRAIN_PER_PASS)` then `serve_remote` for
97	  each (`src/app.rs:1585-1597`). The connection thread answers 429/503/504
98	  without the frame (`src/adapters/remote.rs:787-833`). Static bytes
99	  could be answered on the connection thread the same way (they need no
100	  core state), or on the frame through `serve_remote`. §4.1 "the frame
101	  does core state only" leans toward the connection thread. Not decided
102	  here.

104	### The router (`src/app.rs`)
105	
106	- `serve_remote` (`:3017-3121`) refuses any path without the `/api/v1/`
107	  prefix with 404 `not_found` (`:3023-3025`). Then it answers `info` and
108	  `pair` unauthenticated (`:3027-3031`), authenticates, and handles
109	  `events` (`:3036-3038`) and the allowlist. The static paths would be a
110	  new arm before the prefix match, and they are the third thing served
111	  before pairing (§5's rule, `docs/remote-client.md` l.390 in the
112	  section, "Require pairing before anything but `/info` and `/pair`").
113	- `authenticate` (`:3125-3153`) knows only `request.bearer`. Both its
114	  refusals have the code `unauthorized`, with different messages: "pair
115	  this device first" (no token) and "the token is not known; pair again"
116	  (revoked, rotated, or never valid). **A page cannot tell "revoked"
117	  from "never paired" by the code.** With an HttpOnly cookie, the page
118	  cannot even see whether it holds a token. The "revoked" state in the
119	  issue needs either a distinct code (additive) or a non-secret marker
120	  the page keeps itself (for example, "I paired with server X as device
121	  Y").
122	- `remote_subscribe` (`:2723-2758`) requires `request.upgrade` and a
123	  device. It does not check `Origin`. Neither does anything else.
124	- `remote_pair` (`:3606-3674`) compares the body's `spki_sha256` with the
125	  host's own, then the code, uppercased. It counts a failure on either
126	  (`PairingFailed`). It answers `{token, scope, server_id, device_id}` in
127	  the envelope. A cookie would be set here.
128	- `remote_info` (`:3568-3600`) carries `spki_sha256`, `server_name`,
129	  `capabilities`, `version`, `pairing_open`, but not the device's scope
130	  (it is unauthenticated). The header's "scope" comes from the `/pair`
131	  reply, and after that from nowhere: **no endpoint today tells a device
132	  its current scope**. A scope change in the dialog is invisible until a
133	  `control` command is refused. The Swift client has the same gap.
134	- `refuse` (`:3754-3772`) logs method and path, never the query. A
135	  `GET /?code=…` that reached the router would not log the code. Any
136	  new static handler must keep that true.

207	## Things the issue asserts that the tree contradicts or leaves open
208	
209	- "Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused": true (`src/app.rs:3023`), but
210	  on the frame, after the request was queued (so it costs inbox space),
211	  not at the connection thread.
212	- "the one-line excerpt the card shows" is not on the wire (above).
213	- "the device's scope in the header": no endpoint returns it after
214	  pairing (above).
215	- "'revoked' said plainly": the refusal code does not distinguish it
216	  (above).
217	- The `key` check in the page compares the URL's key with what `/info`
218	  says. A page cannot read the TLS certificate it is talking over, so
219	  this proves only that the host *claims* that key. A relay forwards
220	  `/info` faithfully, and the host's own `spki_sha256` check in
221	  `remote_pair` (`:3639-3647`) is fed by the page's body, which is the
222	  impostor's page under a relay. What it does catch is a genuine page on
223	  the wrong genuine host (a second installation at that address or
224	  port, or a rotated key). The issue says roughly this. The tree adds
225	  that §5's sentence "the host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is
226	  not its own, so a relayed request … fails" does not hold for a
227	  browser, and the spec text must say so.
228	- Cookies are scoped by host, not by port. Two Switchboard instances on
229	  one Mac (`SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT`, design §3.1) and any other HTTPS
230	  service on another port of that host would all receive a
231	  `Secure` cookie set by one of them. A cookie name per `server_id`
232	  avoids the clash between instances. It does not stop another service
233	  on that host from receiving it. `localStorage` is per origin
234	  (scheme, host and port), so it does not have this problem, but any
235	  script on the origin can read it.

A URL parser can fill `addresses` with the one host:port.

17	### Outside the tree
18	
19	- **Apple's TLS server certificate rules.** SHA-2 signature, RSA at least 2048 bits, the server's DNS name in subjectAltName (CommonName not trusted), and for certificates issued after 1 July 2019 an EKU of `serverAuth` and a validity of at most 825 days. Non-compliant connections fail and "websites [may] not load in Safari". Evidence: https://support.apple.com/103769 (iOS 13 / macOS 10.15; Citrix says iOS 14 / macOS 11 also). The page does not mention IP-address SANs, user-added roots, or exemptions. The current certificate has no SAN, a CN only, and a not-after of year 4096 (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`), so it meets none of the SAN, EKU or validity rules.
20	- **Safari and `wss://` after a click-through.** The behaviour exists and is unfixed: WebKit bug 41419 ("allow wss:// if user has accepted https:// warning") is open, status NEW, last modified 2026-01-12, and the reporter got `wss` working only after marking the certificate always-trusted (https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419). code-server's iPad doc agrees: Safari "will prevent WebSocket connections unless the certificate is installed as a profile", needs a domain name rather than a bare IP, and needs a SAN matching the host (https://github.com/cdr/code-server/blob/v3.7.0/doc/ipad.md). Two sources agree; they cover Safari up to 2026-01. One more report is mixed: on iOS 26 beta 3, `wss` failed after acceptance and the poster said it was resolved in beta 5 (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/792842). That is a forum post, a lead only.
21	  - Queries: "Safari iOS WebSocket wss self-signed certificate accepted exception fails fetch works"; "iOS Safari self-signed certificate no subjectAltName IP address proceed certificate warning".
22	- **Secure contexts.** `crypto.randomUUID()` is available only in secure contexts (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Crypto/randomUUID). The spec decides trustworthiness by the origin's scheme: `https` and `wss` are "Potentially Trustworthy", with no mention of certificate errors (https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-secure-contexts/ §3.1; MDN Secure_Contexts agrees). By the text, an https page on a click-through certificate is a secure context. Whether browsers also treat it so is not stated, and it is under Unresolved.

### 4.2 API conventions

- Version prefix: `/api/v1`.
- JSON request and response bodies. Timestamps as milliseconds since the epoch, matching the wire crate (`last_stop_at_ms`); the client formats them.
- The wire crate's views are the response schemas. New views are added to `switchboard-control` additively (it stays std + serde only, and Dispatch keeps compiling).
- Standard error shape: `{ "error": { "code": "...", "message": "..." } }`, with `wire::Reply::Failed` mapped onto it.
- **Every response** carries the host's `epoch` and `revision` (§4.4) in an envelope: `{ "epoch": "...", "revision": n, "body": ... }`. The revision is the one at which the body's **content version** was observed (§4.4, "Content versions"), not merely the counter at the time of the reply. The client keeps one held revision per resource key (a session's metadata, its conversation, its screen, one run's output, one file are separate keys) and applies a reply only if its revision is at or past the held one, so an older reply arriving after a newer one is dropped and fetching a session's metadata never invalidates a valid conversation page.
- **Caps.** The serialized, masked body of any reply is at most 1 MiB, envelope included, enforced on the output bytes. The rule per kind:
  - **collections** (`projects`, `spaces`, `sets`, `sessions`, `runs`, a set's pins, `waiting`) are answered **whole, in one reply, never paged and never cut**. They are small: a data directory holds hundreds of records at most, and a project's session list with every string bounded as below is under 100 KiB at that scale. A collection reply is one snapshot of its membership at one revision, which is what makes a cached member's removal safe: a member missing from a whole reply at a revision at or past the one it was learned at is gone. The 1 MiB cap is enforced on the serialized reply as everywhere; a collection that would exceed it is a bug in the bounds, answered `too_large` and logged, not paged around.
  - **metadata views**, in a collection and standing alone, are bounded field by field, after masking: `notes` at 4 KiB in a collection and 64 KiB standing alone, `name`, `waiting_reason`, `cwd` and every other free-text string at 4 KiB, each cut marked in a `truncated` list of field names; no field is left unbounded. A client that wants a session's full notes reads the session alone.
  - **conversation** pages stop at `limit` turns or at the cap with `next`; a turn larger than 256 KiB is cut and marked (§4.3).
  - **last response** and **run output** are cut from the front (older text dropped) and marked `truncated: true`.
  - **file content** is sent whole or not at all: the port's file limit is 768 KiB of source bytes, and a larger pinned file answers `too_large` with its size. The source limit is not a guarantee of fit: JSON escaping can double a file of quotation marks and masking can lengthen text, so the limit is enforced once more on the masked, serialized reply, and a file that exceeds it there answers `too_large` too, naming the serialized size. The client says so on the card.
  - **screen** is bounded by `lines` (at most 200) and, after masking, by bytes: text over 256 KiB is cut from the top (older lines dropped) and marked `truncated: true`.
- A command is **accepted** when `serve` returns; its outcome arrives through events and the session's state. For `session.send` there is no completion signal beyond the next `Stop` hook event on that record (§4.5).
- Document payload schemas with examples; generate the Swift `Codable` types from the Rust views (serde shapes) and keep a fixture test on both sides.

Everything else on the wire is **refused before translation**, by an allowlist, not a denylist: `env.resolve` returns secret values; the `env.*` writes, `definition.install`, `project.add`, `project.root`, `set.sync`, `workflow.*`, `dispatch.runner`, `session.kill` and `session.remove` change what runs on the host or what it keeps. v1 remote is the table above and nothing more.

**Redaction, one policy for every text that leaves the port, applied before any cut.** `session.screen` today masks the values of the project's secret variables and of the session's granted environment sets, and it reads slack lines above the window first so a value wrapped across the window's first line is still found whole. The port generalizes both halves of that: one `redact` function in `app.rs`, and the rule that **masking runs over complete source text, and every cut comes after**, since a value split by a cut no longer matches. Per kind:
  - **conversation**: the parser caps tool detail at `DETAIL_CAP` while parsing, so masking a parsed turn would miss a value crossing that cap. The transcript reader gains an additive `read_masked(handle, &dyn Fn(&str) -> String)` that applies the mask to every string field before `cap`; the port's conversation cache (§4.4) is populated through it, keyed by the secret set's fingerprint as well, and is separate from the UI's unmasked cache. The 256 KiB turn cut then runs on masked text.
  - **run output**: `scrollback::tail_text` cuts bytes before stripping escapes and choosing lines. It gains an overlap: the read starts `longest secret length` bytes before the tail window, the mask runs over the whole buffer, and the line selection then discards the overlap; a value straddling the window's first byte is therefore masked whole. A secret value containing a newline is masked only within a line, which the dialog's sentence on redaction covers.
  - **screen**: the existing slack-lines read, unchanged.
  - **file content**: the file is read whole under its limit, masked, then sent.
  - **last response** and the card excerpt: masked from the turn's full text, then cut.
  The secret set for a session is the project's secret variables plus its granted sets; for a file it is the owning project's. The set is resolved **before any cached content is returned**, on every read, and its **policy fingerprint** (a hash over the sorted names and values, held in memory only, never logged or stored) is part of every masked cache's version (§4.4): a new grant, a changed value or a removed set makes previously masked bytes stale even when their source did not move. If the secret set cannot be resolved (a Keychain error, a missing set), the reply is **refused** with that reason, never sent unredacted and never served from a cached success. What this covers is exactly the values Switchboard holds: a secret the user pasted into a prompt, or one a tool printed that Switchboard never knew, is not found. The paired-devices dialog says this in a sentence, and the claim in design.md's trust boundary is widened to "or as redacted text on the remote port".

New read models, added to the wire crate:

- `session.conversation`: the `Conversation` from `ports::transcript` as a wire shape: title, model, branch, usage, and turns paged by **turn number** (`n`, 1-based). The host parses the whole JSONL, as the session view does, from the app-level cache (§4.4); a transcript the app can show is one the port can serve, and the supported size is whatever the app handles, which the spike measures. What paging bounds is the **response**: a page anchored at its start (`from=turn`) stops at `limit` turns or at the body cap, whichever first, and says `next` for the turn to continue from; a page anchored at its end (`from=last`, or `before=turn` for the page ending before a turn the client holds) fills backward from the anchor, so it always reaches it and `from` is wherever it filled up. The client opens on the tail and walks back with `before`, so a transcript whose turns are large never shows a stale end or a gap; a change is followed from the last turn held page after page until `next` is empty, up to ten pages. A page carries only the first 512 bytes of each tool call's input and result and of each activity's text, marked `more`, which is what keeps a turn with a hundred tool calls to tens of kilobytes rather than hundreds; `session.turn` reads one turn whole, at the conversation's revision, and the client asks for it when a turn's activity is opened. A single turn larger than 256 KiB is cut (final text kept whole where possible, activity text trimmed) and marked `truncated`. The page carries the `resume_id` it was read from: `/clear` and a discard rebind the record to a new transcript, and a client holding turn numbers from another handle drops them and refetches from 1. The last turn is always in progress until a `Stop` event: on a `changed {conversation}` the client refetches from the last turn it holds and **replaces** that turn and everything after it. A handle rebind (`resume_id` moved on the session view) changes the conversation cache's key, which emits `changed {conversation}` of its own, so the client needs no rule linking the two. Only Claude Code sessions have a conversation; Codex, shell, command and service sessions answer with a "no conversation" reason and the client falls back to `screen` (and, for commands and services, `run_output`).
- `session.last_response`: the last turn's `final_text`, its `n` and `end`. It is a **projection of the `conversation` key**: it is read from the same cache, carries the conversation's content revision, is watched by watching `conversation`, and refreshes on `changed {conversation}`; a window showing only the last response registers that watch. The compact card's one-line excerpt is not part of it: that is `last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the session's metadata, and moves with `changed {session}`.
- `session.runs`: a command's or service's runs as the record holds them (`Run`: `n`, started, ended, exit, artifacts' names, not their paths). `session.run_output`: the tail of one run's scrollback log (`scrollback::tail_text`, escapes stripped, `lines` clamped to 500), redacted; a run whose log was pruned or rotated answers with that reason. This is how an exited command whose pane is gone is still readable: `session.screen` refuses a session that is not running, by design.
- `file.read`: content of a file **only if some working set pins it** (`PinTarget::File` with that project and path). The read goes through a new `ports::files` method, `read_pinned(root, relative)`, not through the UI's preview loader. Confinement is by descriptors, not by path strings, so it stays valid while names change under it:
  - the relative path is rejected if it is absolute, empty, or has a `..` or `.` component, before anything touches the disk (a persisted pin can hold anything);
  - the project root is opened once as a directory descriptor (`O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_CLOEXEC`) and the walk proceeds **one component at a time** with `openat` from the previous descriptor: every directory component with `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`, the last with `O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK | O_CLOEXEC`. A component that is a symlink fails the open (`ELOOP`), so **no symlink anywhere in the path is followed, parent or leaf**; a swap of any directory for a link between two hops is refused at the next hop, and a swap after the hop cannot move the descriptor already held. `openat` comes through a safe wrapper crate (`rustix`; or `cap-std`, which does this walk itself, if the spike prefers it); the crate-wide `unsafe` ban stands;
  - `O_NONBLOCK` on the open is what keeps a FIFO from parking the connection thread for good: the open returns at once, `fstat` on the descriptor must say regular file, and anything else (a FIFO, a socket, a device, a directory as the leaf) is refused before any read. The flag is cleared on the regular file before reading. The read runs on the content worker (§4.1), so even a stall here costs the worker its time, never a frame;
  - the read is `take(limit + 1)` with the port's limit of 768 KiB (§4.2), so growth after the check cannot exceed the limit;
  - dotenv names (`.env`, `.env.*`) are refused whatever is pinned, since those hold the project's secrets;
  - the reply carries the file's `modified` and `size` from the same descriptor, and the content is masked like every other text.
  Both platforms the crate builds on are Unix, so one implementation serves macOS and Linux CI.
- `info`: `server_id`, `server_name`, protocol version, capabilities, `epoch`, `revision`, the certificate's public-key hash (SPKI, SHA-256), the port's limits (file limit, conversation page size, body cap), and whether the pairing window is open.

Avoid a general-purpose filesystem endpoint. Paths are never accepted from the client except as the identity of an existing pin.

### 4.4 WebSocket events

Envelope:

```json
{
  "server_id": "uuid",
  "epoch": "uuid",
  "revision": 1042,
  "type": "changed",
  "resource": {"kind": "session", "id": "record-uuid"},
  "at_ms": 1760220000000
}
```

Event types:

- `hello {epoch, revision}`: the first frame on every subscription.
- **Scope.** A listing leaves out the records Dispatch made for its own use: a ticket's project with everything in it, and a worker session (the planner, an implementer, a reviewer) in any project, told by the `<ticket>-<nonce>` form of the op they were made under (`switchboard_control::is_dispatch_worker_op`). A supervisor's records (`sup-…`) and the owner's own are listed as ever, and a worker record is still read by its id, which is how the ticket view to come will reach them. `?scope=all` on `projects`, `sessions`, `waiting` and on the `events` subscription lists them and announces them; a plain subscription gets no `project`, `sessions`, `session` or `runs` frame about one. `info` lists `scope` among its capabilities. The point is the wire: hundreds of worker sessions on a host, which the headset fetched one project at a time, are now neither fetched nor announced.
- `changed {kind, id}` with the **metadata kinds** `project`, `space`, `set`, `session`; the **content kinds** `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output` (`id` = `record/n`), `file` (a pinned file, `id` = `project_id/path`); and the collection kinds `projects`, `spaces`, `sets` (with the space's id), `sessions` (with the project's id), `runs` (with the record's id), `waiting`, emitted when a collection's member id set moves and answered by refetching the collection whole; a global collection's `id` is the empty string. Each kind is its own resource key on the client (§4.2); a member fetched as part of its collection holds the collection's revision until it is read alone.
- `removed {kind, id}`: the resource is gone; the client drops it and marks any window on it "removed on <server>".
- `watching {kind, id}`: the answer to a `watch` frame (below).
- `resync_required`: sent before the host closes a subscriber whose queue overflowed; the client reconnects and refetches everything.

**What produces events.** The host has no event bus, and a save is not a reliable sign of a visible change: working sets save through `SaveViews`, Claude Code's trust question (`PromptSeen`) and a Codex pane going quiet (`HostListed`) change what a card says with no save at all. So the port does not watch for saves. Revision and events come from three places in `app.rs`:

1. **The read-model diff, after every pass.** After every `dispatch` and after every polling pass (`HostListed`, the hook log, `Tick`), the app recomputes a cheap per-resource fingerprint of each exported metadata read model (`SessionView`, `SetView` with its members, `ProjectView`, `SpaceView`, `waiting`) and compares it with the previous pass's. One `changed` per resource whose fingerprint moved, one `removed` per resource that vanished, one `changed` per collection whose membership moved, and `revision` bumped once per pass that emitted anything. The diff is the gate, not the effect list, so a set rename, a pin edit, a trust-question transition, a quiet-state transition and a time-based rule-set change all surface without anyone naming them. The fingerprint is a hash over the view's serialized bytes **with its time-derived fields held at zero**: `quiet_secs` is computed from the clock in `session_view` and would move every pass, so the view gains an additive `last_activity_ms` the client derives quiet from, and the quiet **state** (the card's word moving to idle) is what the diff sees. Collections carry the membership revision of §4.2, bumped only when the member id set moves. The hash is cheap at this scale (hundreds of records); the spike measures it (§10).
2. **Content versions, assigned where content is read.** Conversation text, pane text, run output and pinned files are mutable outside the core and can change between two reads inside one poll interval, so a content reply's revision cannot come from the counter alone. Every content read goes through a per-key **content cache** in `SwitchboardApp`, whose bookkeeping lives on the frame and whose reads run on the connection or worker thread (§4.1). The cache holds, per key, the **source version** and the **policy fingerprint of the owning project (§4.3)** it last served, with the revision it was assigned. The source version per kind, chosen so that no change the host can see leaves it unchanged:
   - **transcript**: size and mtime. Claude Code's JSONL only appends, Switchboard never edits one, and `/clear` or a discard rebinds the record to another file, so a growing size is a reliable version and a same-size rewrite does not occur;
   - **pinned file**: inode, ctime and size, read from the descriptor the walk ends on. No user tool preserves ctime, so an editor that rewrites in place, a same-size rewrite, and a replace-by-rename (a new inode) all move it;
   - **run output**: inode, ctime and size of the run's log. A log truncated and regrown to the same length has a new ctime; a rotated one a new inode;
   - **screen**: a hash of the pane text, as today.
   When either the source version or the policy fingerprint differs from what the cache holds, the worker's reply carries the new content and the frame, on the worker's version action, bumps `revision`, emits `changed {content kind, id}`, and stores the new version with that revision; the reply is stamped with that revision. **Two different content versions never share a revision for one key within an epoch**, and two reads of unchanged content return the same bytes and the same revision. The policy is resolved before the read; a resolution failure refuses the reply and leaves the cache untouched, so no earlier masked bytes stand in for the answer. A policy change is also noticed by the diff pass (the `env.*` actions are dispatches), which emits `changed` for every watched content key of the affected project without waiting for a read.
3. **The watch poll.** The port keeps a **watch set**: every content key any subscriber has asked to watch, plus every content key read in the last minute. Independently of the local view, every two seconds a worker thread checks each watched key's source version (a `stat`, or a pane snapshot for `screen`; never a parse) and, for a key that moved, reads it through the content cache, which is what emits the `changed`. The local session view reads its conversation through the same cache (an unmasked variant; §4.3), so the two polls share work rather than duplicate it. The set is capped at 128 keys (§4.1); past that the least recently read key is dropped, and a key with no subscriber and no read for a minute is dropped too. A read of a key not in the set still answers and still versions correctly, since the version is checked on every read; what eviction costs is the `changed` event until the next read, which the client's periodic refetch of a visible view covers.

**Watch frames.** A client sends `watch {kind, id}` when the first view instance on a content key opens and `unwatch` when the last one closes; the client keeps a reference count per key so closing one of two windows on a session changes nothing on the host. The host answers `watching` once the key is in its set, and the client fetches the initial content only after that, so the first snapshot's revision is covered by the poll from then on. A watch is never refused. On reconnect, after `hello`, the client resends every watch with a nonzero count before it snapshots. A visible content view also refetches on its own every thirty seconds, which is what covers a key the host evicted from the set.

**The conversation cache** moves from `UiState` to `SwitchboardApp` as one of the content caches, keyed by record id, resume handle and content version, read by the session view and the port alike; `UiState` keeps a reference, not a copy. This is a frontend change (the session, card and workflow views read the cache), so it is its own commit before any port code, Milestone A0 (§10), with the app behaving identically. This, the diff and the worker handoff are the changes to the app outside the adapter, and §12.6 says why they are required.

**Subscribe first, then snapshot.** A client connecting to a host:

1. opens the WebSocket and waits for `hello {epoch, revision}` (events start flowing at once and are buffered by the client);
2. fetches the snapshots it needs, each reply carrying its own `revision`;
3. applies the buffered events: an event whose `revision` is past a snapshot's `revision` invalidates that resource and is refetched; the rest were already in the snapshot;
4. enables commands.

Because the subscriber is registered on the frame thread before any later pass can bump `revision`, a metadata snapshot is taken on that thread with the revision it carries, and a content reply is stamped on that thread when the worker's version action lands (the same moment its `changed` would be emitted, so the event and the reply name one revision), no change can fall between a subscription and a snapshot. Several snapshots in flight are each reconciled against the buffer by their own revision; events that arrive during a refetch are reconciled the same way, which is why the client never clears its buffer until step 4. A resource named by an event the client has never seen is fetched. If `epoch` differs from the one the client holds (the host restarted), every cached item is stale and is refetched. There is no retained-event replay: a `resync_required` is the only answer to a gap, and events are never durable.

One `changed` per resource whose fingerprint moved, one `removed` per resource that vanished, one `changed` per collection whose membership moved, and `revision` bumped once per pass that emitted anything. The diff is the gate, not the effect list, so a set rename, a pin edit, a trust-question transition, a quiet-state transition and a time-based rule-set change all surface without anyone naming them. The fingerprint is a hash over the view's serialized bytes **with its time-derived fields held at zero**: `quiet_secs` is computed from the clock
2. **Content versions, assigned where content is read.** Conversation text, pane text, run output and pinned files are mutable outside the core and can change between two reads inside one poll interval, so a content reply's revision cannot come from the counter alone. Every content read goes through a per-key **content cache** in `SwitchboardApp`, whose bookkeeping lives on the frame and whose reads run on the connection or worker thread (§4.1). The cache holds, per key, the **source version** and the **policy fingerprint of the owning project (§4.3)** it last served, with the revision it was assigned. The source version per kind, chosen so that no change the host can see leaves it unchanged:
   - **transcript**: size and mtime. Claude Code's JSONL only appends, Switchboard never edits one, and `/clear` or a discard rebinds the record to another file, so a growing size is a reliable version and a same-size rewrite does not occur;
   - **pinned file**: inode, ctime and size, read from the descriptor the walk ends on. No user tool preserves ctime, so an editor that rewrites in place, a same-size rewrite, and a replace-by-rename (a new inode) all move it;
   - **run output**: inode, ctime and size of the run's log. A log truncated and regrown to the same length has a new ctime; a rotated one a new inode;
   - **screen**: a hash of the pane text, as today.

The policy is resolved before the read; a resolution failure refuses the reply and leaves the cache untouched, so no earlier masked bytes stand in for the answer. A policy change is also noticed by the diff pass (the `env.*` actions are dispatches), which emits `changed` for every watched content key of the affected project without waiting for a read.
3. **The watch poll.** The port keeps a **watch set**: every content key any subscriber has asked to watch, plus every content key read in the last minute. Independently of the local view, every two seconds a worker thread checks each watched key's source version (a `stat`, or a pane snapshot for `screen`; never a parse) and, for a key that moved, reads it through the content cache, which is what emits the `changed`. The local session view reads its conversation through the same cache (an unmasked variant; §4.3), so the two polls share work rather than duplicate it. The set is capped at 128 keys (§4.1); past that the least recently read key is dropped, and a key with no subscriber and no read for a minute is dropped too. A read of a key not in the set still answers and still versions correctly, since the version is checked on every read; what eviction costs is the `changed` event until t

**Watch frames.** A client sends `watch {kind, id}` when the first view instance on a content key opens and `unwatch` when the last one closes; the client keeps a reference count per key so closing one of two windows on a session changes nothing on the host. The host answers `watching` once the key is in its set, and the client fetches the initial content only after that, so the first snapshot's revision is covered by the poll from then on. A watch is never refused. On reconnect, after `hello`, the client resends every watch with a nonzero count before it snapshots. A visible content view also refetches on its own every thirty seconds, which is what covers a key the host evicted from the set.

**The conversation cache** moves from `UiState` to `SwitchboardApp` as one of the content caches, keyed by record id, resume handle and content version, read by the session view and the port alike; `UiState` keeps a reference, not a copy. This is a frontend change (the session, card and workflow views read the cache), so it is its own commit before any port code, Milestone A0 (§10), with the app behaving identically. This, the diff and the worker handoff are the changes to the app outside the adapter, and §12.6 says why they are required.

**Subscribe first, then snapshot.** A client connecting to a host:

1. opens the WebSocket and waits for `hello {epoch, revision}` (events start flowing at once and are buffered by the client);
2. fetches the snapshots it needs, each reply carrying its own `revision`;
3. applies the buffered events: an event whose `revision` is past a snapshot's `revision` invalidates that resource and is refetched; the rest were already in the snapshot;
4. enables commands.

Because the subscriber is registered on the frame thread before any later pass can bump `revision`, a metadata snapshot is taken on that thread with the revision it carries, and a content reply is stamped on that thread when the worker's version action lands (the same moment its `changed` would be emitted, so the event and the reply name one revision), no change can fall between a subscription and a snapshot. Several snapshots in flight are each reconciled against the buffer by their own revision; events that arrive during a refetch are reconciled the same way, which is why the client never clears its buffer until step 4. A resource named by an event the client has never seen is fetched. If `epoch` differs from the one the client holds (the host restarted), every cached item is stale and is refetched. ### 4.5 Commands

- `send`, `resume` and `trust` are authenticated actions under `control` scope against one owning server and session.
- The client makes a UUID operation id per command and sends it as the wire `op`.
- **Logged before run.** Today `operations.log` gets a request line only for creations, and the reply line after the command ran; `serve` skips a command only when a reply line exists. That leaves a crash between sending keys and appending the reply as a repeat on retry. The port closes that gap for every non-replayable command (`Class::NonReplayable`: `session.send`, `session.resume`): `serve` appends the request line **before** dispatch, and a failed append refuses the command without running it. On arrival, an op with a request line and no reply line is answered `interrupted` and **not run again**; an op with a reply line is answered from it. `session.trust` is `Idempotent` on the wire and needs neither.

  - `done`: use the reply;

  A timeout on a command is followed by a status query, never by a blind resend.

A device does not keep a prompt of its own: it reads the editor's draft and works on it, so dictation from the headset, dictation at the desk and typing on either meet in one text, and a prompt begun on one device can be finished on the other. # Plan: a web control surface on the remote port (#230)

Line numbers are as they are in this worktree at 7fe8949. Schema versions
as they stand today: `SCHEMA_VERSION = 16` (`src/core/model.rs:12`),
`VIEWS_SCHEMA_VERSION = 7` (`:612`), `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1`
(`src/ports/remote.rs:17`). Only the last moves, and it is written below
as "the value in `ports/remote.rs` at implementation time, plus one".
"Facts" means the facts file for this issue; a line cited as Settled N or
Unresolved N is in it.

## Where this departs from the issue

- **"The one-line excerpt the card shows" is not on the wire.**
  `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:636-688`) has no excerpt. The record
  has `last_message` (written by `src/bin/switchboard-hook.rs:37`;
  Settled, tree), but `remote-client.md` §4.3 says the excerpt is
  "masked from the turn's full text, then cut", and masking resolves the
  session's secret set, which §4.1 keeps off the frame. Putting
  `last_message` on `SessionView` would send unmasked text from a frame
  answer. So no `SessionView` change: the page fetches
  `sessions/{id}/last-response` for each Claude session, as the headset
  does (`client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:149-163`), and
  only when that session's `last_stop_at_ms` differs from what it holds.
  No `watch` is registered for these, so the 128-key watch set is not
  touched by the list. Codex, shell, command and service rows show kind
  and state without an excerpt.
- **"The device's scope in the header": no endpoint returns it after
  pairing** (`remote_info`, `src/app.rs:3568`, is unauthenticated; the
  `/pair` reply is the only place, and it goes stale when the owner
  changes the scope in the dialog). The plan adds one authenticated read,
  `GET /api/v1/device`. This is the single new read model; the page
  cannot show a current scope without it.
- **"Revoked said plainly" cannot be told from "never paired" by the
  host's answer.** `authenticate` (`src/app.rs:3127-3153`) refuses both
  with `401 unauthorized`, and with an HttpOnly cookie the page cannot
  see whether it holds a token. The page keeps a non-secret marker
  (`server_id`, `device_id`, key hash, name) in `localStorage`. A 401
  with a marker says "This browser is no longer paired (it was revoked on
  the host, or the browser dropped its cookie). Pair again." A 401 with
  no marker says how to pair. "Identity changed, pair again" is the
  marker's `server_id` matching `/info` with a different key hash.
  No new refusal code.
- **"Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused" is true but late:**
  `serve_remote` refuses it at `src/app.rs:3023`, after the request has
  taken a slot in the 64-deep channel and a frame pass. With a page, a
  browser sends strays (`/favicon.ico`, a prefetch). The connection
  thread now owns this decision: the three page paths are served there, any
  other path outside `/api/v1/` is answered 404 there, and `serve_remote`
  keeps its own refusal as the backstop.
- **"The browser then trusts that certificate for that address" is not
  safe to build on.** Settled (WebKit 41419, code-server's iPad doc): on
  Safari a click-through can cover the page and `fetch` but not `wss://`.
  The page therefore works on REST polling alone and treats the socket as
  an upgrade (decision 1 below).
- **"`history.replaceState` … the code never stays in the history" is
  stronger than the sources.** MDN (Settled) says `replaceState`
  replaces the current entry; it says nothing of what the browser
  recorded before the script ran (Unresolved 6). The plan makes the
  claim the host can keep: the code is single-use and the window closes
  at the first pairing, three failures or five minutes (Settled,
  `src/core/remote.rs:46-72`), so a recorded URL is dead. The dialog says
  that instead of promising the history is clean.

## The record

No new record kind, no `model.rs` change, no `SCHEMA_VERSION` or
`VIEWS_SCHEMA_VERSION` bump. A browser is one more `PairedDevice`
(`src/ports/remote.rs:96-107`) in `devices.json`, which is a bare
`Vec<PairedDevice>` with no version. Its name is the page's `device_name`
("Safari on iPhone", built by the page from `navigator.userAgent`; the
host already cuts it to 64 characters, `new_device`,
`src/core/remote.rs:166-175`). No `kind` field: the name is enough for
the dialog (decision 6) and the host reads no `User-Agent`. Revoke and
scope change already apply on the next request and revoke closes the
socket.

One record changes: `identity.json`. The certificate is reissued over the
same key (Settled: `KeyPair::from_pem` is already used,
`src/adapters/remote.rs:139,146`; the SPKI is of the key, so the pin
and `spki_sha256` do not move, §5). The reason is Settled (Apple's
rules): the current certificate has no subjectAltName, a CN only, no EKU,
and a `not_after` in the year 4096, so it meets none of the SAN, EKU or
825-day rules Safari applies. Reissuing cannot hurt the click-through
path and may help it (Unresolved 1, 2 and 3 are the open questions about
how much), so it does not wait on them. Two additive fields on `Identity`
(`src/ports/remote.rs:26-42`), both `#[serde(default)]`:

- `certificate_names: Vec<String>`: the DNS and IP names the certificate
  carries, sorted.
- `certificate_expires: Option<SystemTime>`.

Bump `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION` to the value in `ports/remote.rs` at
implementation time, plus one. `identity.json` has no migration step:
`load_identity` is a plain deserialize, so an older file reads with the
defaults (an empty list, `None`), which `bind_remote` treats as "reissue
now". Written through the existing atomic `RemoteFiles::save`.

Rehydration is unchanged: `IdentityLoaded` at launch, devices by token
hash on every request. The pairing window stays non-durable. On the
device, what persists is the HttpOnly cookie (script cannot read it) and
the marker in `localStorage` (not secret: ids and a public key hash).
The cookie is the only place the token lives in the browser (decision 2).

## The signals

### Decision 1: browser trust in the certificate

**Picked: the click-through on the local network is the trust step, said
in the dialog. The host does not offer the certificate for download in
this cut.** Why: a download or profile install is a second trust
mechanism with its own surface (a route that serves a certificate before
pairing, a profile format, what iOS asks of a manually trusted
certificate), and the only evidence that it fixes `wss://` on Safari is
two sources of 2021 and 2026 (Settled), against Unresolved 1-3, which no
experiment here can settle. It is the follow-up if owner question A
comes back unfavourable (named at the end).

What the click-through buys, and what it does not (the dialog says this
in two sentences, and §5 of the spec is amended to say it):

- It lets the owner open the page. It proves nothing about who answered.
- The `key` in the URL lets the genuine page refuse to send the code to a
  host whose `/info` presents a different `spki_sha256`. That catches the
  right page on the wrong genuine host (a second installation on that
  address or port, a rotated key). A page served by an impostor is not a
  genuine page and checks nothing; a page cannot read the key of the TLS
  connection it is on, so even the genuine check proves only that the host
  claims that key. §5's sentence "a relayed request through a substituted
  certificate fails" stands for native clients and is amended: it does not
  hold for a browser.
- What bounds the damage: the code is single-use and short-lived
  (Settled), the pairing window shows scope, and the owner sees the new
  device in the dialog and can revoke it.

The reissue (above) gives the certificate `serverAuth`, a validity of 800
days (under 825, Unresolved 3: if the rule does not bind a manually
trusted leaf, nothing is lost), and SANs for `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`,
the outward address from `local_address()` as an IP SAN, and, on macOS,
`<LocalHostName>.local` as a DNS SAN (Unresolved 2 and 9: both forms are
present, so whichever Safari accepts is there). The dialog says the
certificate is renewed (key, and so pin, unchanged) and that a changed
address means a new browser warning (Unresolved 7).

The page's default is REST polling every 5 seconds plus a refetch of the
open session. When `new WebSocket` opens, the page switches to events
and stops polling; when it fails or closes, the page says "Live updates
unavailable, refreshing every 5 s" and polls. This is the same page
whether Unresolved 1 comes back favourable or not; the socket is the
enhancement, built behind the polling and not in front of it.
`crypto.randomUUID` is used only when `window.isSecureContext`, with a
`getRandomValues` fallback otherwise (Unresolved 4).

### Decision 2: how the token reaches the host

**Picked: an `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` cookie, set by the
`/pair` reply, carried by `fetch` and by the socket handshake. The page's
script never sees the token. Nothing in `localStorage`, no subprotocol
token.** That is the safer store (a script on the origin can read
`localStorage`; it cannot read an HttpOnly cookie), so it is the one this
plan builds. The facts file's Owner D says the server accepts all three
transports; this plan builds one (plus the bearer header the native
clients use) and does not build the other two.

Mechanics that are unresolved are the implementer's first test, before
any other page code (Unresolved 5): on Safari, Chrome and Firefox with the
reissued certificate, does a `Secure` cookie set by `/pair` over an IP
host come back on a same-origin `fetch`? (This is the basic behaviour; the
`__Host-` prefix needs `Secure`, `Path=/`, no `Domain`, all met.) Does it
come back on a same-origin `new WebSocket` handshake? If the `fetch` half
fails, the finding goes to the owner as a follow-up and no
`localStorage` or subprotocol transport is added in this commit. If only
the socket half fails, nothing changes: the page polls (decision 1).

Host side:

- `read_request` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:444-513`) keeps three more
  headers, as the bearer is kept, so none are logged with the rest:
  `cookie`, `origin`, `host`. `RemoteRequest` (`:360`) gains
  `cookie: Option<String>`, `origin: Option<String>`,
  `host: Option<String>`. Settled: only `adapters/remote.rs` builds it,
  and no test constructs it.
- The token is the bearer if present, else the cookie named
  `__Host-sb-<server_id>` (per-installation name: Settled says cookies are
  not isolated by port, so two instances on one Mac would otherwise
  collide). `authenticate` (`src/app.rs:3127`) takes it from a new
  `RemoteRequest::token(&self, server_id)`; the cookie value is checked
  for length and base64url characters before it is hashed.
- **Origin check.** A cookie is ambient: `SameSite=Strict` is by site, and
  a site includes every port on the host, so another page on another port
  of this Mac is same-site. For a request authenticated by the cookie (no
  bearer), any method but GET and any WebSocket upgrade must carry an
  `Origin` equal to `https://` + the request's `Host` header, compared
  case-insensitively; otherwise `403 forbidden_origin`, no side effect.
  Comparing with the `Host` header, not a list of addresses, is what makes
  this correct for an IP, a `.local` name or loopback. Bearer-authenticated
  requests are exempt: a header is not ambient. This answers the owner
  question on `Origin`, and it is a security decision, so it is decided
  here.
- **`/pair`** (`remote_pair`, `src/app.rs:3606`) takes an additive body
  field `"transport": "cookie"`. With it the reply omits `token`, and
  `RemoteReply` carries `Set-Cookie: __Host-sb-<server_id>=<token>;
  Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Max-Age=34560000` (400 days,
  the longest browsers keep). Without it the reply is unchanged, so the
  CLI and the headset are untouched. `RemoteReply` (`:389`) gains
  `set_cookie: Option<String>` and `#[derive(Default)]`; Settled says it
  is built literally at about 15 sites in `src/app.rs` and none in `tests/`,
  so each literal gets `..RemoteReply::default()`, a mechanical edit.
- The cookie goes to every HTTPS service on that host, on any port
  (Settled). It is `HttpOnly`, so it cannot be read by script; it can be
  sent to a service the owner runs on the same Mac. The dialog says so, and
  it is named for the owner at the end.

### Decision 3: one QR

**One URL.** The pairing window's QR and "Copy invite" carry
`https://<ip>:<port>/?code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>`,
built by one pure function in `src/core/remote.rs`,
`invite_url(address: SocketAddr, identity, code)`. It formats the address
through `SocketAddr`, so an IPv6 result gets its brackets (the JSON form
did not). Code, key and id are Crockford, hex and a UUID: nothing needs
percent-encoding. The JSON form is no longer emitted. Settled: the
visionOS paste field, `ConnectionManager.swift`, `BrowserView.swift:106,
883` and the CLI all go through `PairingInvite.parse`
(`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:114`), so only that
changes: it tries `URLComponents` first (`code`, `key`, `id`, and
`addresses = ["host:port"]`) and the existing JSON decode second, so an
invite copied before the update still pairs. `addresses` stays a list
(`ConnectionManager.swift:483`, `main.swift:120`). The `.local` name is not
put in the URL: owner question B decides that, and the IP works whichever
way it comes back.

### Decision 4: the static paths

- **Paths, exactly:** `GET /` (also with a query), `GET /app.js`,
  `GET /app.css`. Content types `text/html; charset=utf-8`,
  `text/javascript; charset=utf-8`, `text/css; charset=utf-8`. The HTML
  carries `<link rel="icon" href="data:,">` so no `/favicon.ico` request is
  made. Any other method on these is `405` with `Allow: GET`; any other
  path outside `/api/v1/` is `404` with the usual JSON error.
- **Headers on all three (and the 404/405):** `Content-Security-Policy:
  default-src 'none'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; connect-src
  'self'; img-src data:; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none';
  frame-ancestors 'none'`, `Cache-Control: no-store`,
  `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` (the URL with the code must not leave in
  a `Referer`), `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Connection: close`.
  The page has no inline script, no inline style and no `style=` attribute,
  and no external URL. Whether WebKit treats `connect-src 'self'` as
  covering `wss://` on the same host is not in the facts; the first
  manual run on Safari records it, and the polling path is why a "no" does
  not break the page.
- **Who answers:** the connection thread (`connection`,
  `src/adapters/remote.rs:770`), before the request is handed to the
  frame, because the bytes need no core state and §4.1 says the frame does
  core state only. The bytes are `include_str!("../../web/index.html")`,
  `app.js`, `app.css` in `adapters/remote.rs`. No build step, no
  dependency.
- **Pool and rate window.** A page load counts against the 4
  unauthenticated connections like any stranger (§4.1; unchanged), and
  `Connection: close` frees the slot as soon as the file is sent, so the
  three files do not hold three slots for 30 s of idle (Unresolved 8: how
  many parallel connections iOS Safari opens needs a device). Static paths get
  their own `RateWindow` in `Limits` (`:625-640`), 60 per minute per
  listener, `429` past it, so a page-load loop cannot be charged to the
  `/pair` window (6/min) or the `/info` window (60/min). The page's own
  `/info` and `/pair` calls count against theirs as today.
- **Before pairing the listener serves `/info`, `/pair` and the page.**
  §5's "Require pairing before anything but `/info` and `/pair`" is
  amended to add the page. The page's bytes are identical on every
  installation and carry no host data (no id, no key, no name): the
  host-specific values arrive only in the URL the owner scanned and in
  `/info`.
- **Opened with neither code nor marker:** a plain message: "Open
  Remote devices in Switchboard on the Mac, choose Allow pairing, and scan
  the code with this device's camera." No code-entry form in this cut: a
  typed code without the scanned key would skip the one check the page
  can make. A paste field is the natural follow-up.
- **`refuse` and the code.** The page request never reaches the frame, so
  `refuse` (`src/app.rs:3754`, logs method and path only) is not on the
  path; the static arm logs nothing and never logs the query.

### The page's protocol (`web/app.js`)

Order on load: (1) if `location.search` has `code`, hold `code`, `key`,
`id` in variables and call `history.replaceState(null, "",
location.pathname)` as the first statement; (2) `GET /api/v1/info`;
(3) with a code: refuse to continue unless `info.spki_sha256 === key` and
`info.server_id === id`, else say "this is not the host whose code was
scanned" and send nothing; (4) `POST /api/v1/pair {code, device_name,
spki_sha256, transport: "cookie"}`; on success store the marker and
continue, on `403 pairing_closed|wrong_code|wrong_key` say which, plainly;
(5) with no code and a marker: if `info.server_id` equals the marker's and
the key differs, "identity changed, pair again" and send nothing; (6)
`GET /api/v1/device` for the name and current scope; a 401 is the revoked
or never-paired state above.

After that it speaks §4.2 and §4.4: every reply is the envelope
`{epoch, revision, body}`; one held revision per resource key (a project's
session list, one session, one session's `conversation` or `screen`); a
reply is applied only at or past the held revision; a changed `epoch`
refetches everything. Subscribe first, then snapshot: open
`wss://<host>/api/v1/events`, wait for `hello`, fetch `projects` and each
`projects/{id}/sessions` (at most 4 in flight), then apply buffered events
by revision. `changed {session}` refetches that session and re-sorts;
`changed {sessions, project}` refetches that project; `changed {projects}`
refetches the list; `removed` drops it; `resync_required` reconnects and
refetches. Opening a session sends `watch {kind: "conversation", id}` for a
Claude session or `watch {kind: "screen", id}` otherwise, waits for
`watching`, then fetches `last-response` or `screen`; leaving sends
`unwatch`. Refetch the open view every 30 s regardless (§4.4, covers
eviction). Without the socket, every poll refetches the list and the open
view; the held-revision rule is the same.

A reply is `POST sessions/{id}/send {op, text}` under `control`, with the
op made per command. On a timeout the page asks `GET ops/{op}` and follows
§4.5: `done` uses the reply, `interrupted` shows the session's state and
never resubmits, `unknown` resubmits with the same op. A session with
`trust_question` shows "Waiting at Claude Code's folder trust question;
answer it on the Mac" and no box; one with `prompt_refusal` shows the box
disabled with that reason. Trust, resume, new session, the draft,
dictation, Dispatch tickets and the conversation beyond the last response
are not on the page (owner question; the API serves them).

### `GET /api/v1/device`

Authenticated, any scope. Reply, in the envelope: `{device_id, name,
scope, server_id}`, read from the core's current device, so a scope change
in the dialog shows on the next call. Handled in `serve_remote`
(`src/app.rs:3017`) after `authenticate` and before the allowlist match,
beside `events`, with no `wire::Body`. No fixture: Swift does not decode
it (the fixtures exist for Swift and Rust to agree, and nothing on the
Swift side reads this).

## The actions and effects

One new action, `AppAction::CertificateReissued { certificate: String,
names: Vec<String>, expires: SystemTime }`, handled in
`src/core/remote.rs` through the existing `update_identity`
(`:105-117`), which already emits `Effect::SaveIdentity` and does nothing
when read-only. No new effect, no new port method: `RemoteStore` already
saves the identity.

Adapter: `remote::reissue_certificate(identity, key_pem, names, now) ->
Result<(String, SystemTime), String>` beside `make_identity`
(`src/adapters/remote.rs:95`), over `KeyPair::from_pem`, with the SANs,
`serverAuth`, `not_before` a day back, `not_after` 800 days out; and
`remote::local_names()`, the sorted names above (the `.local` name from
`scutil --get LocalHostName`, absent when the command fails or off macOS,
so Linux CI compiles and passes). In `bind_remote` (`src/app.rs:2935`),
before `tls_config` at `:2957`: if `identity.certificate_names` differs
from `local_names()`, or `certificate_expires` is `None` or within 30 days,
call `reissue_certificate` with the Keychain key already fetched there,
dispatch `CertificateReissued`, and build the TLS config from the core's
identity afterwards. `make_identity` also fills the two new fields. An
address that changes while the port is running is not noticed until the
next bind; that is a known gap in the design status, not machinery here.

Serving the page is not an effect: it never leaves the connection thread.
The request-side changes (three headers, `set_cookie`, the Origin check)
are in the adapter and `authenticate`, with no action.

## The UI

**The pairing window** (`src/ui/remote.rs:155-215`). The `json!` payload
and `qr_texture` input become `core::remote::invite_url(...)`; "Copy
invite" copies the URL and its hover says "The QR code's link, to open in
a browser or paste into a client". The caption keeps the key and code and
gains the trust text from decision 1 (two sentences: the browser will warn
about this host's certificate; accepting it is the step that trusts this
network and does not verify the host; the key in the link only stops a
page from sending the code to a different Switchboard; the link works
once and expires in five minutes or three wrong codes). The paired-devices
section (`devices`, `:230`) gains one line under the table: a browser's
token is an HttpOnly cookie sent to any HTTPS service on this Mac's
address. It uses `GAP` and `PAD`; no logic beyond the format call.

**The page** (`web/index.html`, `app.js`, `app.css`), one file each, no
framework. A header with the host's name (from `/info`), the device's
name and scope word (from `/device`), and the live/polling indicator.
Below: a "Waiting on you" group first (every session with `waiting`,

## The signals

### Decision 1: browser trust in the certificate

**Picked: the click-through on the local network is the trust step, said
in the dialog. The host does not offer the certificate for download in
this cut.** Why: a download or profile install is a second trust
mechanism with its own surface (a route that serves a certificate before
pairing, a profile format, what iOS asks of a manually trusted
certificate), and the only evidence that it fixes `wss://` on Safari is
two sources of 2021 and 2026 (Settled), against Unresolved 1-3, which no
experiment here can settle. It is the follow-up if owner question A
comes back unfavourable (named at the end).

What the click-through buys, and what it does not (the dialog says this
in two sentences, and §5 of the spec is amended to say it):

- It lets the owner open the page. It proves nothing about who answered.
- The `key` in the URL lets the genuine page refuse to send the code to a
  host whose `/info` presents a different `spki_sha256`. That catches the
  right page on the wrong genuine host (a second installation on that
  address or port, a rotated key). A page served by an impostor is not a
  genuine page and checks nothing; a page cannot read the key of the TLS
  connection it is on, so even the genuine check proves only that the host
  claims that key. §5's sentence "a relayed request through a substituted
  certificate fails" stands for native clients and is amended: it does not
  hold for a browser.
- What bounds the damage: the code is single-use and short-lived
  (Settled), the pairing window shows scope, and the owner sees the new
  device in the dialog and can revoke it.

The reissue (above) gives the certificate `serverAuth`, a validity of 800
days (under 825, Unresolved 3: if the rule does not bind a manually
trusted leaf, nothing is lost), and SANs for `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`,
the outward address from `local_address()` as an IP SAN, and, on macOS,
`<LocalHostName>.local` as a DNS SAN (Unresolved 2 and 9: both forms are
present, so whichever Safari accepts is there). The dialog says the
certificate is renewed (key, and so pin, unchanged) and that a changed
address means a new browser warning (Unresolved 7).

The page's default is REST polling every 5 seconds plus a refetch of the
open session. When `new WebSocket` opens, the page switches to events
and stops polling; when it fails or closes, the page says "Live updates
unavailable, refreshing every 5 s" and polls. This is the same page
whether Unresolved 1 comes back favourable or not; the socket is the
enhancement, built behind the polling and not in front of it.
`crypto.randomUUID` is used only when `window.isSecureContext`, with a
`getRandomValues` fallback otherwise (Unresolved 4).

**Picked: an `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` cookie, set by the
`/pair` reply, carried by `fetch` and by the socket handshake. The page's
script never sees the token. Nothing in `localStorage`, no subprotocol

`localStorage`; it cannot read an HttpOnly cookie), so it is the one this
plan builds. The facts file's Owner D says the server accepts all three
transports; this plan builds one (plus the bearer header the native
clients use) and does not build the other two.

Mechanics that are unresolved are the implementer's first test, before
any other page code (Unresolved 5): on Safari, Chrome and Firefox with the

come back on a same-origin `new WebSocket` handshake? If the `fetch` half
fails, the finding goes to the owner as a follow-up and no
`localStorage` or subprotocol transport is added in this commit. If only
the socket half fails, nothing changes: the page polls (decision 1).

  `cookie`, `origin`, `host`. `RemoteRequest` (`:360`) gains
  `cookie: Option<String>`, `origin: Option<String>`,

  and no test constructs it.

  not isolated by port, so two instances on one Mac would otherwise

  covering `wss://` on the same host is not in the facts; the first
  manual run on Safari records it, and the polling path is why a "no" does
  not break the page.

  frame, because the bytes need no core state and §4.1 says the frame does
  core state only. The bytes are `include_str!("../../web/index.html")`,

  dependency.
- **Pool and rate window.** A page load counts against the 4
  unauthenticated connections like any stranger (§4.1; unchanged), and
  `Connection: close` frees the slot as soon as the file is sent, so the
  three files do not hold three slots for 30 s of idle (Unresolved 8: how
  many parallel connections iOS Safari opens needs a device). Static paths get
  their own `RateWindow` in `Limits` (`:625-640`), 60 per minute per
  listener, `429` past it, so a page-load loop cannot be charged to the
  `/pair` window (6/min) or the `/info` window (60/min). The page's own
  `/info` and `/pair` calls count against theirs as today.
- **Before pairing the listener serves `/info`, `/pair` and the page.**
  §5's "Require pairing before anything but `/info` and `/pair`" is
  amended to add the page. The page's bytes are identical on every
  installation and carry no host data (no id, no key, no name): the
  host-specific values arrive only in the URL the owner scanned and in
  `/info`.
- **Opened with neither code nor marker:** a plain message: "Open
  Remote devices in Switchboard on the Mac, choose Allow pairing, and scan
  the code with this device's camera." No code-entry form in this cut: a
  typed code without the scanned key would skip the one check the page
  can make. A paste field is the natural follow-up.
- **`refuse` and the code.** The page request never reaches the frame, so

### The page's protocol (`web/app.js`)

Order on load: (1) if `location.search` has `code`, hold `code`, `key`,
`id` in variables and call `history.replaceState(null, "",
location.pathname)` as the first statement; (2) `GET /api/v1/info`;
(3) with a code: refuse to continue unless `info.spki_sha256 === key` and
`info.server_id === id`, else say "this is not the host whose code was
scanned" and send nothing; (4) `POST /api/v1/pair {code, device_name,
spki_sha256, transport: "cookie"}`; on success store the marker and
continue, on `403 pairing_closed|wrong_code|wrong_key` say which, plainly;
(5) with no code and a marker: if `info.server_id` equals the marker's and
the key differs, "identity changed, pair again" and send nothing; (6)
`GET /api/v1/device` for the name and current scope; a 401 is the revoked
or never-paired state above.

After that it speaks §4.2 and §4.4: every reply is the envelope
`{epoch, revision, body}`; one held revision per resource key (a project's
session list, one session, one session's `conversation` or `screen`); a
reply is applied only at or past the held revision; a changed `epoch`
refetches everything. Subscribe first, then snapshot: open
`wss://<host>/api/v1/events`, wait for `hello`, fetch `projects` and each
`projects/{id}/sessions` (at most 4 in flight), then apply buffered events
by revision. `changed {session}` refetches that session and re-sorts;
`changed {sessions, project}` refetches that project; `changed {projects}`
refetches the list; `removed` drops it; `resync_required` reconnects and
refetches. Opening a session sends `watch {kind: "conversation", id}` for a
Claude session or `watch {kind: "screen", id}` otherwise, waits for
`watching`, then fetches `last-response` or `screen`; leaving sends
`unwatch`. Refetch the open view every 30 s regardless (§4.4, covers
eviction). Without the socket, every poll refetches the list and the open
view; the held-revision rule is the same.

A reply is `POST sessions/{id}/send {op, text}` under `control`, with the
op made per command. On a timeout the page asks `GET ops/{op}` and follows
§4.5: `done` uses the reply, `interrupted` shows the session's state and
never resubmits, `unknown` resubmits with the same op. A session with
`trust_question` shows "Waiting at Claude Code's folder trust question;
answer it on the Mac" and no box; one with `prompt_refusal` shows the box
disabled with that reason. Trust, resume, new session, the draft,
dictation, Dispatch tickets and the conversation beyond the last response
are not on the page (owner question; the API serves them).

Authenticated, any scope. Reply, in the envelope: `{device_id, name,
scope, server_id}`, read from the core's current device, so a scope change
in the dialog shows on the next call. Handled in `serve_remote`
(`src/app.rs:3017`) after `authenticate` and before the allowlist match,
beside `events`, with no `wire::Body`. No fixture: Swift does not decode
it (the fixtures exist for Swift and Rust to agree, and nothing on the
Swift side reads this).

as they stand today: `SCHEMA_VERSION = 16` (`src/core/model.rs:12`),

  `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:636-688`) has no excerpt. The record

  "masked from the turn's full text, then cut", and masking resolves the
  session's secret set, which §4.1 keeps off the frame. Putting
  `last_message` on `SessionView` would send unmasked text from a frame
  answer. So no `SessionView` change: the page fetches
  `sessions/{id}/last-response` for each Claude session, as the headset
  does (`client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:149-163`), and
  only when that session's `last_stop_at_ms` differs from what it holds.
  No `watch` is registered for these, so the 128-key watch set is not
  touched by the list. Codex, shell, command and service rows show kind
  and state without an excerpt.
- **"The device's scope in the header": no endpoint returns it after
  pairing** (`remote_info`, `src/app.rs:3568`, is unauthenticated; the
  `/pair` reply is the only place, and it goes stale when the owner
  changes the scope in the dialog). The plan adds one authenticated read,
  `GET /api/v1/device`. This is the single new read model; the page
  cannot show a current scope without it.
- **"Revoked said plainly" cannot be told from "never paired" by the
  host's answer.** `authenticate` (`src/app.rs:3127-3153`) refuses both
  with `401 unauthorized`, and with an HttpOnly cookie the page cannot
  see whether it holds a token. The page keeps a non-secret marker
  (`server_id`, `device_id`, key hash, name) in `localStorage`. A 401
  with a marker says "This browser is no longer paired (it was revoked on
  the host, or the browser dropped its cookie). Pair again." A 401 with
  no marker says how to pair. "Identity changed, pair again" is the
  marker's `server_id` matching `/info` with a different key hash.
  No new refusal code.
- **"Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused" is true but late:**
  `serve_remote` refuses it at `src/app.rs:3023`, after the request has
  taken a slot in the 64-deep channel and a frame pass. With a page, a
  browser sends strays (`/favicon.ico`, a prefetch). The connection
  thread now owns this decision: the three page paths are served there, any
  other path outside `/api/v1/` is answered 404 there, and `serve_remote`
  keeps its own refusal as the backstop.
- **"The browser then trusts that certificate for that address" is not
  safe to build on.** Settled (WebKit 41419, code-server's iPad doc): on
  Safari a click-through can cover the page and `fetch` but not `wss://`.

  an upgrade (decision 1 below).
